entertainment.title: Goldman Sachs Thinks the Sports Boom Isn’t Going Anywhere
entertainment.summary: The investment bank released a new report exploring how media rights and athlete fame will help drive the business higher.
entertainment.body:
Within most media companies, sports remain core to their larger content strategy. Premium entertainment isn’t going anywhere, of course, but if you ask Ted Sarandos or Mike Cavanagh or Josh D’Amaro about their content mix, sports will be at the center of it.

“These events break through,” Sarandos said on the company’s last earnings call. “They drive new membership, they add fuel to our ad revenues.”

It’s with that backdrop that Goldman Sachs is releasing a new report focused on sports investing … and the bank is predicting that the sports economy is only going to go up from here.

“We increasingly hear from our clients a continuation of a theme that started with our first paper two years ago, which is this really high level of interest in participating in this explosion that we’re seeing in the sports ecosystem,” says Goldman Sachs partner Nicole Pullen Ross. “When you think about the trajectory of growth within sports, our expectation is that we’ll see growth within the sports ecosystem grow to you know over $600 billion by 2030, that’s 44 percent growth.”

Indeed, the new Goldman report notes a number of things contributing to that explosive growth, from continually rising media rights deals (the bank estimates global sports media rights will hit $67 billion this year); institutional capital buying into teams; and all the ancillary opportunities around entertainment and live events and IP.

Goldman also dug into some more sector-wide (and in some cases economywide) trends: Institutional investors are buying into teams as league change their roles to give owners more liquidity, and sports team owners, like many business owners, are exploring how artificial intelligence can improve efficiency and create more personalized fan experiences.

But the report also digs into the ancillary opportunities in sports, particularly around athlete-centric brands (athlete-led studios and consumer brands, etc) shortform content, and opportunities like VR tickets to games.

“In an increasingly fragmented media landscape, sports owners are leveraging the power of storytelling to capture and retain a fan base with an increasingly short attention span,” the report states. “Rather than relying solely on traditional broadcasts, they use narrative-driven content to sustain the appeal of live games while capturing younger demographics.”

entertainment.title: ‘Occupational Hazard’ Rock Doc Details the Untold Story of Jimmy Buffett’s ‘Ragtag,’ Pre-Fame Coral Reefer Band
entertainment.summary: "Those were wild times," says director John H. Cunningham.
entertainment.body:
The Coral Reefer Band is as intrinsically a part of the Jimmy Buffett universe as the E Street Band is to Bruce Springsteen’s, the Heartbreakers are to Tom Petty’s and so on. Explore Jimmy Buffett See latest videos, charts and news

But a largely untold portion of the band’s story is the focus of the new documentary Occupational Hazard: The First Coral Reefers , which, after a nearly nine-month run in film festivals and theaters, becomes available Oct. 30 for rent via Apple TV, Amazon Prime Video, Google Play and Fandango. Related Selena Gomez Celebrates 'Ups & Downs' With Demi Lovato: 'I'm Proud of What We've Been Through' Meet Leah Barylsky, the Woman Behind the Camera - And On the Stage -- During Rüfüs Du Sol's Record-Breaking Tour Will My Chemical Romance Score Its First No. 1 Album Next Week (With a 20-Year-Old Album)?

As the title indicates, Occupational Hazard is an origin story, from the beginnings of Buffett’s career as a troubadour (after a tenure writing for Billboard ) and his move to Key West, Florida, where he assembled the initial Coral Reefer lineup during the mid-70s. (He used the name for an imaginary band during his solo performances before then.) Narrated by actor and Buffett friend Jeff Bridges, it details a decidedly different and significantly less polished ensemble than Parrotheads became used to from the late ‘70s until Buffett’s death on Sept. 1, 2023.

The portrayal is of a time when the Coral Reefer crew was wasted but not really wasting away, as Buffett registered defining tracks such as “Margaritaville,” “Cheeseburger in Paradise,” “Volcano,” “Fins” and “Son of a Son of a Sailor.”

“We wanted to capture the time before the Parrothead phenomenon began, when it was still rough ‘n’ ready out on the road” director-producer John H. Cunningham tells Billboard via Zoom. “Those were wild times; many viewers who are watching this have no idea that period even existed for this band, because they’ve seen this very organized, polished group for such a long time,” he says. “But the first years were a little bit different. Some of the band are starting to pass away and disappear without the history being recorded. So just for historical purposes, we thought this was an important time to document.”

Original Coral Reefer Roger Bartlett, who composed the film’s score, readily acknowledges that “we were fully staffed with artificial inspiration…in great quantities” during that time. But the guitarist, who performed with Buffett as an acoustic duo before the band formed, also maintains that “the early days were really the best days” for other reasons.

entertainment.title: Eric Karson, Director of ‘The Octagon’ and Producer of ‘Lionheart,’ Dies at 86
entertainment.summary: The son of a TV writer, he also worked with French kickboxer Olivier Gruner on two films and with Tom Skerritt on one.
entertainment.body:
Eric Karson, the martial-arts movie specialist who directed Chuck Norris in The Octagon and produced the Jean-Claude Van Damme-starring Lionheart , has died. He was 86.

Karson died Aug. 24 of natural causes while in hospice care in Henderson, Nevada, his brother Gil Karson told The Hollywood Reporter .

Karson also directed Olivier Gruner in his first movie, Angel Town (1990), and produced his second film, Nemesis (1992), and the French kickboxer considered Karson a mentor. Related Stories Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist Movies Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies at 86

The son of a TV writer, Karson was working for Los Angeles-based American Cinema Productions when he was offered the chance to make his feature directorial debut on The Octagon (1980).

Written by Leigh Chapman of Dirty Mary Crazy Larry fame at the dawn of the ninja movie craze, the film stars Norris as Scott James, a retired karate champion who takes on a band of assassins led by his estranged foster brother (Tadashi Yamashita).

At Imperial Entertainment, Karson directed Van Damme in Black Eagle (1988), then reunited with the Belgian martial artist on Lionheart (1990), directed by Sheldon Lettich.

With his turn as Lyon Gaultier, who deserts the French Foreign Legion and becomes a street fighter to raise money for his murdered brother’s family, Van Damme became a leading man in the U.S.

One of four kids, Karson was born in Phoenix on March 5, 1940. His father was Lee Karson, who created the 1956-59 CBS-ABC program The Gale Storm Show (also known as Oh, Susanna ), set on a ship à la The Love Boat ; he also wrote for shows including The Restless Gun , Wagon Train and The Detectives . His mother, Mary, was a theater actress turned homemaker.

entertainment.title: Christina Hendricks, Accidental DJ, Has Music Lovers Lining Up
entertainment.summary: The actress is embracing a longtime passion with packed live sets and a guest radio residency at KRCW. Her song choices are a siren call for Millennials and Gen X.
entertainment.body:
The queue outside of the auditorium snaked nearly 200 people long. This wasn’t an unusual sight for the South Pasadena concert hall from bookers and promoters Sid the Cat. Their year-old destination , housed inside a 19th Century elementary school, has already hosted Sylvan Esso, Mike D, Death Cab for Cutie and Jenny Lewis side hustle Nice as Fuck. But on the October Saturday in question, the stage inside Sid the Cat Auditorium was empty. Instead, the crowd was there for actress Christina Hendricks at the venue’s bar. Most would expect Hendricks, the instantly recognizable redhead from Mad Men , Drive and Good Girls , to be there performing a one-woman show. Maybe some experimental theater. Perhaps she’s just joined the legion of celebrities with their own line of spirits. But they clearly don’t know Hendricks, because she was there to DJ. “Everyone who knows me says, ‘Oh yeah, this makes perfect sense,’” Hendricks tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Because I’ve been doing this since junior high, making playlists and forcing them upon people. This is my favorite thing.” Related Stories Movies 'Ancestors' Invites You to a Cinematic "Séance," Led by Éanna Hardwicke, That Mixes Dream, Reality and Memory (Exclusive TIFF Clip and Chat) TV Naomie Harris and Christina Hendricks Filming BBC Legal Drama 'Reputation'

Rumblings of “DJ Christina Hendricks” began earlier in 2026 after she made two appearances at San Diego listening bar Part Time Lover. Her debut was a bit of a fluke at the coaxing of her close friend, the harpist and DJ Mary Lattimore. She suggested Hendricks bring some of her own records down from Los Angeles. She’d show her the ropes and they’d share billing. Hendricks says she balked for a split second before she recognized the kind of wish fulfillment that was on the table. Each played for two hours. Hendricks proved a quick study and Part Time Lover asked her back. But with Lattimore busy, she decided to go it alone. She was getting comfortable with the gear, and it felt like a relatively low-pressure scenario.

“When we started walking towards the venue, my husband went, ‘I think there’s a line out front,’” says Hendricks, who’s married to cinematographer George Bianchini. “I said, ‘Oh no, sweetie, that must be for restaurants and stuff.’ As we got closer, he was like, ‘No, I’m pretty sure that’s a line for you.’ That’s when I started feeling pressure.”

If she’s still feeling pressure, it appears to be eclipsed by the kick she’s getting out of all of this. At Sid’s Bar, a former classroom in the 140-year-old building, Hendricks looked gleeful as she navigated a playlist that meandered between Shoegaze, Chillwave, Electronic and Indie Sleeze. The crowd, which appeared to lean heavy on 30-to-50-somethings, nodded in approval. And when Hendricks transitioned from Washed Out to The Knife, this geriatric millennial, for one, felt very seen.

entertainment.title: Edinburgh Film Festival Toasts Bollywood With ‘Kuch Kuch Hota Hai’ Anniversary Event at 2028 Edition
entertainment.summary: Superstars of Indian cinema Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol lead Karan Johar's cult favorite.
entertainment.body:
Bollywood is coming to the Edinburgh International Film Festival .

EIFF on Friday confirmed that a special 30th anniversary celebration of the legendary Indian film Kuch Kuch Hota Hai (1998) will screen as part of the 2028 edition.

Partly filmed in Scotland, the beloved cult favorite — and Karan Johar’s directorial debut, following the love triangle between Rahul Khanna ( Shah Rukh Khan ), Anjali Sharma ( Kajol ) and Tina Malhotra (Rani Mukerji) — will return to the cinema to celebrate its enduring legacy as a landmark of Indian cinema, with Johar and other guests in attendance. Related Stories Movies From 'Sh*t Happens' to an Erotic Photographer Being Confronted by His Daughter: Offbeat Films at Tallinn Movies Jamie Dornan Boards 'Nostalgie,' Starring Aidan Gillen as Washed-up Pop Star, as Executive Producer (Exclusive)

Johar was invited to mark Kuch Kuch Hota Hai ‘s anniversary at the 2028 EIFF during a meeting he hosted in the Mumbai offices of his production company, Dharma Productions, earlier this week with the First Minister of Scotland, John Swinney, and Screen Scotland’s interim executive director, David Smith.

The meeting, said EIFF, was focused on Scotland’s potential as a destination and partner for Indian film and television production, co-production, talent development and cultural exchange. Kuch Kuch Hota Hai was the first major Indian production to film extensively across Scotland, including Eilean Donan Castle, Glen Coe, Tantallon Castle and Inchmahome Priory.

Swinney said: “It was a pleasure to meet Karan Johar in Mumbai […] I look forward to welcoming him to Edinburgh. During my visit to India, I met with people from the Indian film industry, including representatives from Dharma Productions, to discuss opportunities for future collaboration between Scottish and Indian filmmaking. Scotland’s screen industry has tremendous potential as a creative partner for Indian film and television, offering the infrastructure, expertise and world-class filming locations to support a wide range of productions.”

EIFF CEO and festival director Paul Ridd said his team is always thinking about the future and what’s next. “So we jumped at an opportunity like this,” he said, “to plant the seeds for a celebration of a legendary, much-loved film at our festival, a film featuring Scotland and some of the most iconic stars of Bollywood cinema on screen. We can’t wait for what promises to be something truly special for our 81st edition in 2028. But in the meantime, watch this space for more news of our 80th next August.”
